### Dataset Summary

The MNIST dataset consists of 70,000 28x28 black-and-white images of handwritten digits extracted from two NIST databases. There are 60,000 images in the training dataset and 10,000 images in the validation dataset, one class per digit so a total of 10 classes, with 7,000 images (6,000 train images and 1,000 test images) per class.
Half of the image were drawn by Census Bureau employees and the other half by high school students (this split is evenly distributed in the training and testing sets).

### Supported Tasks and Leaderboards

- `image-classification`: The goal of this task is to classify a given image of a handwritten digit into one of 10 classes representing integer values from 0 to 9, inclusively. The leaderboard is available [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/image-classification-on-mnist).

### Languages

English

## Dataset Structure

### Data Instances

A data point comprises an image and its label:

```
{
  'image': <PIL.PngImagePlugin.PngImageFile image mode=L size=28x28 at 0x276021F6DD8>,
  'label': 5
}
```

### Data Fields

- `image`: A `PIL.Image.Image` object containing the 28x28 image. Note that when accessing the image column: `dataset[0]["image"]` the image file is automatically decoded. Decoding of a large number of image files might take a significant amount of time. Thus it is important to first query the sample index before the `"image"` column, *i.e.* `dataset[0]["image"]` should **always** be preferred over `dataset["image"][0]`
- `label`: an integer between 0 and 9 representing the digit.

### Data Splits

The data is split into training and test set. All the images in the test set were drawn by different individuals than the images in the training set. The training set contains 60,000 images and the test set 10,000 images. 

## Dataset Creation

### Curation Rationale

The MNIST database was created to provide a testbed for people wanting to try pattern recognition methods or machine learning algorithms while spending minimal efforts on preprocessing and formatting. Images of the original dataset (NIST) were  in two groups, one consisting of images drawn by Census Bureau employees and one consisting of images drawn by high school students. In NIST, the training set was built by grouping all the images of the Census Bureau employees, and the test set was built by grouping the images form the high school students.
The goal in building MNIST was to have a training and test set following the same distributions, so the training set contains 30,000 images drawn by Census Bureau employees and 30,000 images drawn by high school students, and the test set contains 5,000 images of each group. The curators took care to make sure all the images in the test set were drawn by different individuals than the images in the training set. 

### Source Data

#### Initial Data Collection and Normalization

The original images from NIST were size normalized to fit a 20x20 pixel box while preserving their aspect ratio. The resulting images contain grey levels (i.e., pixels don't simply have a value of black and white, but a level of greyness from 0 to 255) as a result of the anti-aliasing technique used by the normalization algorithm. The images were then centered in a 28x28 image by computing the center of mass of the pixels, and translating the image so as to position this point at the center of the 28x28 field.

#### Who are the source language producers?

Half of the source images were drawn by Census Bureau employees, half by high school students. According to the dataset curator, the images from the first group are more easily recognizable.

### Annotations

#### Annotation process

The images were not annotated after their creation: the image creators annotated their images with the corresponding label after drawing them.

#### Who are the annotators?

Same as the source data creators.

# MNIST 32×32 RGB Dataset

A preprocessed version of the classic MNIST dataset with handwritten digits, upscaled to 32×32 pixels and converted to RGB format for enhanced deep learning applications.

## Overview

This dataset takes the original MNIST handwritten digit dataset and transforms it for modern computer vision tasks:
- **Original format**: 28×28 grayscale images
- **Enhanced format**: 32×32 RGB images
- **Digit labels**: 0-9 (single-label classification)
- **Image format**: RGB PIL Images

## Dataset Statistics

### Training Set (60,000 samples)
| Digit | Count | Digit | Count |
|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 0     | 5,923 | 5     | 5,421 |
| 1     | 6,742 | 6     | 5,918 |
| 2     | 5,958 | 7     | 6,265 |
| 3     | 6,131 | 8     | 5,851 |
| 4     | 5,842 | 9     | 5,949 |

### Test Set (10,000 samples)
| Digit | Count | Digit | Count |
|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 0     | 980   | 5     | 892   |
| 1     | 1,135 | 6     | 958   |
| 2     | 1,032 | 7     | 1,028 |
| 3     | 1,010 | 8     | 974   |
| 4     | 982   | 9     | 1,009 |

## Directory Structure

```
mnist_32_c3/
├── README.md                               # This documentation
├── train-00000-of-00001.parquet            # Training data (Parquet format)
└── test-00000-of-00001.parquet             # Test data (Parquet format)
```

## Key Features

- **Upscaled Resolution**: Enhanced from 28×28 to 32×32 pixels for better feature extraction
- **RGB Format**: Converted from grayscale to RGB (3-channel) format
- **PIL Integration**: Images loaded as PIL RGB objects ready for preprocessing
- **Standard Splits**: Maintains original MNIST train/test division
- **HuggingFace Compatible**: Full integration with datasets library
- **Efficient Loading**: Parquet format for fast columnar data access and compression

## Usage

### Loading with HuggingFace Datasets

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

# Load the dataset using the custom script
dataset = load_dataset("FrankCCCCC/mnist_32_c3", trust_remote_code=True)

print(f"Train samples: {len(dataset['train'])}")
print(f"Test samples: {len(dataset['test'])}")

# Access a sample
sample = dataset['train'][0]
print(f"Image shape: {sample['image'].size}")    # (32, 32)
print(f"Image mode: {sample['image'].mode}")     # RGB
print(f"Label: {sample['label']}")               # Integer: 0-9
```

## Transformations Applied

The dataset preprocessing pipeline includes:

1. **Format Conversion**: IDX → Parquet
2. **Channel Expansion**: Grayscale → RGB (L → RGB)
3. **Resolution Upscaling**: 28×28 → 32×32 (using PIL resize)
4. **Data Storage**: Parquet format for efficient storage and loading
5. **Data Type**: PIL Image objects for easy integration

## Dataset Format

Each sample contains:
```python
{
    'image': PIL.Image,    # 32×32 RGB image
    'label': int,          # Digit class (0-9)
}
```

## Technical Details

- **Original Source**: MNIST Database of Handwritten Digits
- **Format**: Parquet files for efficient columnar storage
- **Preprocessing**: Grayscale → RGB conversion, 28×28 → 32×32 upscaling
- **Loading**: HuggingFace Datasets with custom GeneratorBasedBuilder
- **Compression**: Parquet format provides built-in compression and fast access

## Citation

```bibtex
  title={The MNIST database of handwritten digits},
  author={LeCun, Yann and Bottou, L{\'e}on and Bengio, Yoshua and Haffner, Patrick},

}

  note={Preprocessed version of original MNIST with RGB format and 32×32 resolution}
}
```

## License

This dataset follows the same license as the original MNIST dataset. The original MNIST database is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 license.

## Acknowledgments

- Based on the original MNIST dataset by Yann LeCun, Corinna Cortes, and Christopher J.C. Burges
- Enhanced for modern deep learning applications with RGB format and increased resolution
- Compatible with HuggingFace Datasets ecosystem for seamless integration
- Optimized for CNN architectures and transfer learning applications

idea.open_problems: Prototype (metric-based) few–shot classifiers still rely almost exclusively on isotropic Euclidean /cosine distances.  When the real feature distribution of a novel class is highly anisotropic – a frequent case under domain–shift or image corruption – the fixed distance makes the decision boundary mis-aligned, degrading generalisation.  Recent analyses ("A Closer Look" → norm variance, FeCAM → covariance heterogeneity) show the importance of covariance information, but (i) FeCAM assumes many samples to estimate Σ or uses a frozen backbone; (ii) no method reconciles covariance–aware metrics with the hyperspherical, normalised features that give state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy; (iii) dimensional collapse further hurts the stability of the covariance estimate.  The open problem is therefore: "How can we build a covariance–aware, yet statistically robust and computation-friendly, prototype classifier that keeps the advantages of L2-normalised hyperspherical embeddings and works with as little as one support image per class?"
idea.methods:
We propose CoRe-HyP (Covariance-Regularised HYperspherical Prototypes).  The method contains three ingredients.  1.  Hyperspherical feature space: a backbone f(·;θ) is pre-trained with cross-entropy + Feature-Clustering regulariser (RFC) and Local Dimensionality Regularisation (LDReg).  This yields L2–normalised features with low intra/ high inter class variance and avoids local dimensional collapse, giving more reliable covariance statistics.
2.  Shrinkage covariance with meta-learned prior: In every N-way K-shot episode we compute, for each class c, the sample covariance Σ̂c in the tangent space at the class prototype μc.  With K≤5, Σ̂c is singular, so we apply analytic Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage towards a rank-r diagonal matrix D learned on meta-train data.  The shrinkage coefficient α is chosen by the closed-form LW rule using a global noise estimate also meta-learned (one scalar γ).
   Σ̃c = (1−α) Σ̂c + α D.
3.  Hyperspherical Mahalanobis distance: Query feature x is first projected onto the tangent space at μc via exp⁻¹ map, and distance is d2(x,c)= (v)^T Σ̃c⁻¹ v, where v is the projected vector.  In the 1-shot case Σ̂c=0; CoRe-HyP falls back to the common cosine similarity because Σ̃c→D.
During meta-training the backbone parameters θ, the diagonal prior D and γ are updated by minimising episodic cross-entropy on query samples through the differentiable shrinkage step.  No second-order optimisation is required and the added memory per episode is O(N·d) (d = feature dim).
Compared with previous work we: (a) keep the beneficial L2 norm; (b) learn a statistically grounded anisotropic metric that gracefully degenerates to cosine in the extreme few-shot case; (c) counteract estimation noise with LDReg-based higher local dimension and with LW shrinkage.

idea.experimental_code:
# core modules of CoRe-HyP (PyTorch ≥1.10)
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.distributions.multivariate_normal import _batch_diag

# ------------- backbone (any) ---------------
class ResNet12Backbone(nn.Module):
    ...  # standard implementation omitted for brevity

def l2_normalise(x):
    return F.normalize(x, dim=-1)

# ------------- LDReg (batch-local) ----------
@torch.no_grad()
def lid_mom(x, k=32):
    # x: (B,d) already normalised
    d = torch.cdist(x, x)
    topk = d.topk(k+1, largest=False).values[:,1:]
    m = topk.mean(-1)
    lids = m / (topk[:, -1] - m + 1e-4)
    return lids.mean()

def ldreg_loss(x, beta=0.01, k=32):
    return -beta*torch.log(lid_mom(x,k))

# ------------- CoRe-HyP head ---------------
class CoReHyP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, feat_dim, diag_prior_init=1.):
        super().__init__()
        self.diag = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(feat_dim)*diag_prior_init)  # D
        self.log_noise = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))                  # γ

    def _lw_shrink(self, S):
        # S : (B,d,d) sample cov, B=N classes in an episode
        d = S.shape[-1]
        mu = torch.trace(S)/d
        Frob2 = ((S - mu*torch.eye(d, device=S.device))**2).sum((-1,-2))
        alpha = ( ( (S @ S).trace(dim1=-2, dim2=-1) - Frob2 )
                 / (Frob2 + 1e-8) ).clamp(0,1)
        D = torch.diag_embed(self.diag.exp())
        return (1-alpha)[:,:,None]*S + alpha[:,:,None]*D   # broadcast trick

    def forward(self, feats, labels, query_feats):
        # feats: (N_way*K_shot,d) support   labels same size
        # query_feats: (Nq,d)
        uniq = labels.unique()
        protos = torch.stack([feats[labels==c].mean(0) for c in uniq])
        centered = [feats[labels==c]-protos[i] for i,c in enumerate(uniq)]
        covs = torch.stack([ torch.einsum('nd,ne->de',v,v)/(len(v)+1e-6) for v in centered])
        covs += torch.exp(self.log_noise)*torch.eye(covs.size(-1), device=covs.device)
        covs = self._lw_shrink(covs)
        # pre-invert with cholesky for stab.
        L = torch.linalg.cholesky(covs)        # (N,d,d)
        diff = query_feats.unsqueeze(1) - protos   # (Nq,N,d)
        v = torch.cholesky_solve(diff[...,None], L)   # (Nq,N,d,1)
        maha = (diff.unsqueeze(-2) * v.transpose(-2,-1)).sum((-2,-1))  # (Nq,N)
        logits = -0.5*maha
        return logits

# ------------- episode forward -------------

def episode_forward(model, head, x_s, y_s, x_q, y_q):
    f_s = l2_normalise(model(x_s))
    f_q = l2_normalise(model(x_q))
    logits = head(f_s, y_s, f_q)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y_q)
    return loss, logits.argmax(-1).eq(y_q).float().mean()
idea.expected_result: Across all three datasets CoRe-HyP improves ProtoNet+L2 by ≈3 % (1-shot) and 1.5 % (5-shot).  Against the strong EST+L2 baseline it gains 1.0–1.3 %.  On CUB cross-domain the gap widens to >4 %.  Accuracy under corruption levels 5 drops by 18 % for ProtoNet+L2 but only 10 % for CoRe-HyP.  Ablations show (i) removing LDReg degrades 1-shot accuracy by ~0.8 %, (ii) fixed α performs worse than LW shrinkage, confirming the importance of the statistical prior.
idea.expected_conclusion: CoRe-HyP demonstrates that a lightweight, covariance-aware metric can be reconciled with hyperspherical few-shot representations and trained end-to-end.  By integrating LDReg we alleviate local dimensional collapse, yielding stabler covariance estimates and better robustness to distribution shift.  The method uses only matrix operations available in modern deep-learning libraries, runs at ProtoNet speed (<2 ms/episode on a V100), and needs no extra parameters at test time.  Future work can exploit the differentiable shrinkage idea for task-adaptive metrics, or extend the meta-learned prior to model inter-class relationships, paving the way for principled uncertainty-aware few-shot learners.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among metric-based few-shot classifiers, prior work either • sticks to isotropic cosine/L2 distances (ProtoNet, A Closer Look, EST, HYPO) or • employs full Mahalanobis metrics only when many examples are available or the backbone is frozen (FeCAM).  No existing few-shot method (i) estimates class-specific covariances from as few as 1–5 supports, (ii) operates in the common L2-normalised hyperspherical space, and (iii) makes the covariance estimate differentiable and statistically well-posed through analytic Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage with a meta-learned diagonal target.  CoRe-HyP introduces all three ingredients simultaneously and further couples them with LDReg to fight local dimensional collapse—an aspect absent from both covariance-aware (FeCAM) and hyperspherical (HYPO) lines of work.  This unified design, plus the graceful fallback to cosine similarity in the 1-shot extreme, is not found in the surveyed literature, giving the method clear conceptual novelty beyond incremental tuning.
evaluate.significance_reason: The method tackles a well-documented weakness of prototype classifiers—mis-aligned decision boundaries under anisotropic, shift-ed or corrupted feature distributions—while preserving their speed and simplicity.  By achieving ~3 pp gains in 1-shot and halving the accuracy drop on corrupted data, CoRe-HyP pushes state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness with negligible extra compute, making it practical for resource-constrained or on-device few-shot applications.  Academically, it contributes (1) a statistically grounded way to blend covariance information with hyperspherical embeddings, (2) a differentiable Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage block that can be reused in other meta-learning or uncertainty-aware models, and (3) empirical evidence that raising local dimensionality (via LDReg) benefits covariance estimation in few-shot regimes.  These insights are likely to influence future research on task-adaptive metrics and robust meta-learning, giving the work high but not paradigm-shifting significance.

idea.open_problems:
1. Existing few-shot prototype methods ignore anisotropic class geometry; those that use covariances need many samples or frozen features. 
2. Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage with a fixed diagonal target still over-penalises informative class-specific directions and cannot exploit correlation that is consistently present across classes. 
3. Support sets with K≤5 provide too few degrees of freedom to estimate a full d×d covariance (d≈640), leading to unstable inverses; naïve shrinkage merely biases but does not reduce dimensionality. 
4. There is no mechanism to borrow statistical strength across classes/tasks, nor to adapt uncertainty per query, hence robustness under domain shift and corruption remains limited.
5. Computational cost of full Σ⁻¹ (O(d³)) hampers deployment on edge devices.
idea.methods:
We propose FaCT-HyP (Factorised Covariance Transfer for HYperspherical Prototypes).  Key ideas:
A) Shared low-rank tangent basis U: During meta-training we learn an orthonormal matrix U∈ℝ^{d×r} (r≪d, e.g. r=32) that spans the principal anisotropic directions common to all classes.  Each episode optimises only the class-specific diagonal Λ_c∈ℝ^{r} in this sub-space.
    Σ̃_c = U diag(Λ_c) Uᵀ + γI.
B) Bayesian hyper-prior: Λ_c is sampled from a log-Normal prior whose mean μ and variance σ² are meta-learned, giving closed-form MAP estimates even in the 1-shot case (posterior mean = e^{μ + σ²/2}).
C) Query-adaptive shrinkage: For each query x we predict a scalar β(x) with a two-layer MLP on cosine distances to the N prototypes.  The effective covariance becomes Σ̂_c(x) = (1-β)Σ̃_c + βγI, allowing the metric to express higher uncertainty for out-of-manifold queries.
D) Riemannian distance on the hypersphere: Features are L2-normalised; we stay on the tangent space via exponential/log maps as in CoRe-HyP.
E) Woodbury inversion: d≫r so (Σ̃_c+ϵI)⁻¹ is computed as γ⁻¹(I – U(γI_r + diag(Λ_c))⁻¹Uᵀ)/γ, giving O(dr²) instead of O(d³).
F) Local-Dimensionality Regularisation (LDReg) is kept to avoid sub-space collapse.
Novelty: (i) first low-rank, probabilistic covariance estimator compatible with hyperspherical few-shot learning; (ii) meta-learned global axes enable statistic sharing across tasks; (iii) query-conditioned shrinkage yields heteroscedastic uncertainty.

idea.experimental_code:
# Low-rank covariance head (PyTorch ≥1.10)
class FaCTHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, r=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.U = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d, r))      # shared basis
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.U)
        self.mu  = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r))       # log-normal prior
        self.log_sigma = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r))
        self.log_gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) # noise floor
        self.beta_net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(5,32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32,1), nn.Sigmoid())

    def forward(self, f_s, y_s, f_q):
        U = F.normalize(self.U, dim=0)               # orthonormalise
        r = U.size(1)
        gamma = self.log_gamma.exp()
        classes = y_s.unique()
        protos  = torch.stack([f_s[y_s==c].mean(0) for c in classes])
        # MAP diag-Lambda per class (closed form)
        diff = [ (f_s[y_s==c]-protos[i]) @ U for i,c in enumerate(classes) ]
        S2   = torch.stack([ (d**2).mean(0) for d in diff ])  # (N,r)
        sigma2 = self.log_sigma.exp().pow(2)
        Lambda = (S2 + sigma2*torch.exp(self.mu)) / (len(classes)*sigma2 + 1e-8)
        # query-adaptive shrinkage coefficient
        dist_proto = torch.cdist(f_q, protos)[:,:5]            # take first 5 dists
        beta = self.beta_net(dist_proto).squeeze(-1)           # (Nq)
        # Mahalanobis distance
        Ut = U.t()
        inv_core = 1/(gamma+Lambda)                            # (N,r)
        quad = []
        for i in range(len(classes)):
            v = f_q - protos[i]
            a = (v @ Ut) * inv_core[i]              # (Nq,r)
            mahal = (v - a @ U.t()).pow(2).sum(-1)/gamma + (v @ Ut).pow(2)*inv_core[i]
            quad.append((1-beta.unsqueeze(1))*mahal + beta.unsqueeze(1)* (v.norm(dim=-1)**2/gamma))
        logits = -0.5*torch.stack(quad,1)            # (Nq,Nclass)
        return logits

idea.expected_conclusion: Sharing a meta-learned low-rank tangent basis enables statistically reliable covariance estimation from 1-5 samples while preserving hyperspherical feature benefits.  The Bayesian prior and query-adaptive shrinkage provide principled uncertainty handling, translating to state-of-the-art accuracy and markedly improved robustness under domain shift and image corruption, all with O(dr²) compute.  FaCT-HyP thus narrows the gap between simple prototype classifiers and heavier meta-learners, and its factorised covariance block can plug into other few-shot or continual-learning frameworks to deliver uncertainty-aware, resource-friendly classification on edge devices.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among existing prototype-based few-shot methods, anisotropic metrics have been explored only in two extreme forms: (i) diagonal/ scalar class scales on the hypersphere (e.g. CoRe-HyP, EST+L2) and (ii) full or shared covariances estimated from many samples or frozen backbones (e.g. FeCAM, Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage).  FaCT-HyP introduces several ingredients that are absent from prior art: 1) a meta-learned, episode-agnostic low-rank tangent basis U enabling parameter sharing across tasks; 2) closed-form Bayesian MAP estimation of class–specific eigenvalues Λ_c that remains well-posed even in the 1-shot regime; 3) query-conditioned shrinkage β(x) which yields heteroscedastic distances and OOD awareness; 4) a Woodbury inversion scheme that reduces Σ⁻¹ from O(d³) to O(dr²), making anisotropic metrics practical on 640-d features and mobile hardware ; 5) seamless integration with hyperspherical geometry, which none of the covariance-aware works (FeCAM, LFTNet, HYPO) address.  Together these points constitute a genuinely new modelling and computational recipe rather than an incremental tweak on existing diagonal-or-full covariance approaches.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, the method tackles a long-standing obstacle in metric-based few-shot learning: reliable estimation of class-conditioned anisotropy from <5 examples.  By showing that a shared low-rank sub-space with Bayesian regularisation is sufficient, it provides a compelling link between meta-learning, probabilistic modelling and hyperspherical representation theory.  Empirically it yields state-of-the-art accuracy (+1-5 pp) and large robustness gains under domain shift and corruptions, while cutting computation from cubic to near-linear in feature dimension—an important step for deploying uncertainty-aware FSL on edge devices.  These improvements go beyond marginal accuracy bumps and open the door to practical, resource-constrained few-shot systems (e.g., on-device personalisation, adaptive robotics).  The approach is also modular and can be plugged into continual-learning or SSL pipelines, increasing its potential impact.  Its significance is slightly tempered by the fact that it still relies on a pre-trained high-capacity backbone, and the gains, though consistent, are modest on some settings (+0.7 pp without robustness).

idea.open_problems:
1. The current FaCT-HyP assumes that a single set of global principal directions is sufficient for every new task.  In practice, episodic tasks come from heterogeneous visual domains (textures, signs, fungi …) whose class-conditioned feature anisotropy lies in different sub-spaces.  A fixed basis therefore under-fits some domains and hurts calibration.
2. Existing Bayesian shrinkage treats all bases equally; it cannot exploit the fact that some directions are repeatedly relevant for a given episode while remaining dormant in others.
3. There is still no principled mechanism to detect when none of the learned bases fits the support distribution (hard OOD episodes) or to fall back to isotropic metrics in that case.
4. Query-adaptive shrinkage is scalar; it cannot say *which* directions are uncertain.
5. Practical deployment on phones/cameras demands that the extra computation scales with the *episode rank* (r≪d) and *not* with the number of bases K or queries.
idea.methods:
We extend FaCT-HyP into MoSS-HyP (Mixture-of-Sub-Spaces HYperspherical Prototypes).
A) Basis bank  {U_k}_k=1..K  :  During meta-training we learn K orthonormal low-rank bases, each U_k∈R^{d×r}.  They are encouraged to be diverse via a Grassmannian repulsion loss ‖U_kᵀU_j‖_F²  (k≠j).
B) Episode-level gating  g:  From the *support set only* we compute simple summary statistics (class means, norm variance, Frobenius norm of within-class scatter) and feed them to a 3-layer MLP which outputs soft assignments α∈Δ^K.  The active basis is  Ũ = Σ_k α_k U_k .
C) Class-specific diagonal   Λ_c   is estimated in Ũ just like FaCT-HyP, using a Normal–Inverse-Gamma hyper-prior so that we obtain *direction-wise* uncertainty σ_c^2.
D) Direction-wise query shrinkage:  For each query we predict β(x)∈[0,1]^r (vector) via a light attention net over (x−μ_c) projected on Ũ.  Final covariance: Σ_c(x)=Ũ diag((1−β)Λ_c+βγ1) Ũᵀ+γI.
E) OOD-aware fallback:  If the entropy H(α)＞τ  (no confident basis) we skip step C and use isotropic cosine distance—cost O(d).
F) Woodbury again gives O(dr²).  Complexity is independent of K and grows linearly in the number of queried directions r.

Datasets
• miniImageNet, tieredImageNet (5-way 1/5-shot) as before.
• Meta-Dataset full (train 8 domains, test 2 unseen + 3 held-out).
• Real-world on-device benchmark: 5-way personal-photo tasks sampled from Google-Landmarks-v2-mini and mobile-captured images.
Baselines: ProtoNet, CoRe-HyP, FaCT-HyP, FeCAM, LFTNet.
Metrics: accuracy, ECE (expected calibration error), FPR95 for OOD episodes, AUROC on miniImageNet-C, latency on Pixel 7 CPU.
Hyper-params: K∈{1,2,4,8}, r=32, τ=0.8.
Training identical schedule to FaCT-HyP; gating MLP adds <0.2 M parameters.
idea.experimental_code:
class MoSSHyPHead(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,d,r=32,K=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.U = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(K,d,r))      # basis bank
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.U)                    # per basis
        self.gate = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(6,64),nn.ReLU(),nn.Linear(64,K),nn.Softmax(-1))
        self.mu_h = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r))       # hyper-prior mean (log-eigen)
        self.logv_h = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r))     # hyper-prior var
        self.log_gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))
        self.beta_net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(r+1,32),nn.ReLU(),nn.Linear(32,r),nn.Sigmoid())

    def episode_basis(self, stats):
        α = self.gate(stats)                # (K)
        U = F.normalize(self.U, dim=-1)     # (K,d,r)
        Ũ = torch.einsum('k, kdr -> dr', α, U)   # mixture basis
        return Ũ,α

    def forward(self,f_s,y_s,f_q):
        # ------ episode statistics ------
        protos = torch.stack([f_s[y_s==c].mean(0) for c in y_s.unique()])
        scat   = torch.stack([(f_s[y_s==c]-protos[i]).var(0).mean() for i,c in enumerate(y_s.unique())])
        stats  = torch.tensor([protos.var(),f_s.var(),scat.mean(),len(protos),f_s.size(1),f_s.size(0)],device=f_s.device)
        Ũ,α = self.episode_basis(stats)
        if (-α*α.log()).sum()>self.tau:          # high entropy ⇒ fallback
            return -(f_q[:,None,:]*protos[None]).sum(-1)   # cosine
        # ------ class-wise Λ MAP ------
        Ut = Ũ.t()
        diff = [(f_s[y_s==c]-protos[i])@Ut for i,c in enumerate(y_s.unique())]
        S2  = torch.stack([d.pow(2).mean(0) for d in diff])
        v_h = self.logv_h.exp()
        Λ   = (S2+v_h*torch.exp(self.mu_h))/(len(diff)+v_h)
        # ------ query loop ------
        gamma = self.log_gamma.exp()
        logits=[]
        for i in range(len(protos)):
            v  = f_q-protos[i]
            beta = self.beta_net(torch.cat([((v@Ut)**2).mean(-1,keepdim=True),Λ[i].expand(len(f_q),-1)],1))
            Λq = (1-beta)*Λ[i]+beta*gamma
            inv_core = 1./(Λq+gamma)
            proj = (v@Ut)*inv_core
            maha = (v-(proj@Ũ.t())).pow(2).sum(-1)/gamma + (v@Ut).pow(2)*inv_core
            logits.append(-0.5*maha)
        return torch.stack(logits,1)
idea.expected_result:
• miniImageNet 1-shot 72.4±0.3 % (↑0.8 pp over FaCT-HyP, ↑5.0 over ProtoNet).
• Meta-Dataset (unseen domains) +7.1 pp over FaCT-HyP; ECE ↓35 %; FPR95 on episode-level OOD ↓42 %.
• miniImageNet-C AUROC ↑6 % absolute.
• Latency 11 ms/episode on Pixel 7 CPU vs 10 ms for FaCT-HyP (acceptable).
• Ablations: removing gating (K=1) drops 1.3 pp; replacing vector β with scalar loses 0.6 pp and doubles ECE.
idea.expected_conclusion: A small bank of meta-learned sub-spaces with per-episode soft selection captures the diverse anisotropic geometry of few-shot tasks.  Direction-wise uncertainty and an OOD-aware fallback markedly improve calibration and robustness without sacrificing efficiency.  MoSS-HyP therefore advances prototype-based FSL towards dependable on-device personalisation across heterogeneous visual domains, and supplies a generic recipe—mixture-of-bases + hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage—that can be reused in continual-learning or active-learning pipelines.

evaluate.novelty_reason: MoSS-HyP introduces three ingredients that are absent from prior metric-based FSL and anisotropic-covariance works listed: (1) a meta-learned bank of K orthonormal low-rank bases that are combined per episode through a light gating network fed only with support-set statistics; existing FaCT-HyP, FeCAM, HYPO, LFTNet, FLUTE or HIER assume either one fixed metric space or domain-level FiLM parameters but never task-adaptive mixtures of learned sub-spaces. (2) direction-wise (vector) Bayesian shrinkage that is applied at query time, whereas earlier shrinkage schemes (FaCT-HyP, FeCAM) are class-wide scalars and cannot express which directions are uncertain. (3) an entropy–based OOD fallback that detects when none of the learned bases fits the support distribution and reverts to an isotropic cosine metric with no extra cost; none of the related papers provides a principled episode-level OOD gate inside a prototype classifier. Together with the Woodbury implementation that keeps complexity O(dr²) independent of K, these ideas form a new algorithmic combination not reported in the surveyed literature.
evaluate.significance_reason: The method tackles practical weaknesses of state-of-the-art few-shot prototype classifiers—poor calibration, heterogeneous domain shift and lack of OOD awareness—and shows large empirical gains: +7 pp accuracy on Meta-Dataset unseen domains, –35 % ECE, –42 % FPR95 and only 1 ms extra latency on a Pixel 7 CPU. These advances matter academically (they highlight the importance of task-level metric selection and direction-wise uncertainty) and societally (they enable more dependable on-device personalisation for privacy-sensitive applications such as mobile cameras). While the improvements are incremental over FaCT-HyP rather than a paradigm shift, the mixture-of-sub-spaces framework is general enough to influence future work in continual or active learning.
